pages.title: Purpose of a Medical Summary
pages.text:
Legal support help

Purpose of a Medical Summary

A medical summary is a key part of a personal injury case, consolidating a client’s medical history, injuries, treatments, and ongoing needs into a clear, organized format. It supports damage evaluation, case strategy, and accurate presentation.

pages.title: 1. Provides a Snapshot of the Client’s Treatment and Injuries
pages.text:
Legal support help

1. Provides a Snapshot of the Client’s Treatment and Injuries

A medical summary condenses complex, technical records into a clear, coherent overview, turning detailed clinical information into an understandable storyline.

Key Functions in This Area

Clarifies the nature and extent of injuries
Highlights major events in treatment
Tracks recovery progress or complications
Identifies ongoing symptoms and long-term effects

pages.title: 2. Supports Demand Letters, Settlement Negotiations, and Case Preparation
pages.text:
Legal support help

2. Supports Demand Letters, Settlement Negotiations, and Case Preparation

A well-prepared medical summary directly strengthens the legal and strategic aspects of a personal injury claim.

A. Use in Demand Letters

B. Use in Settlement Negotiations

C. Use in Case Preparation and Litigation

Foundation for damages
Provides a clear narrative
Shows organization and credibility

Helps articulate the strength of the case
Allows quick reference during negotiation
Supports higher valuation

Assists in preparing deposition questions
Helps organize exhibits
Supports expert review
Ensures consistency in the case theory

pages.title: Summarizing Medical Records for a Narrative Medical Summary
pages.text:
Legal support help

Summarizing Medical Records for a Narrative Medical Summary

A narrative medical summary presents a client’s treatment in a clear, chronological or provider-based story, organizing clinical details into a readable format for case preparation, demand letters, or litigation.

pages.title: 1. Key Elements to Include for Each Visit
pages.text:
Legal support help

1. Key Elements to Include for Each Visit

Every visit documented in the medical summary should include the following:

1. Date of Service (DOS)

2. Chief Complaint (CC)

3. History of Present Illness (HPI)

4. Examination Findings and Observations

5. Diagnostics Performed

6. Diagnosis

7. Treatment Provided

8. Plan of Care / Recommendations

pages.title: 2. Special Considerations for Physical Therapy or Chiropractic Care
pages.text:
Legal support help

2. Special Considerations for Physical Therapy or Chiropractic Care

1. Initial Evaluation

2. Session Tracking

3. Discharge Summary or Final Report

Record the total number of sessions completed.
Note any missed or cancelled appointments if relevant.

Include functional improvements, limitations, and final assessment.
Highlight remaining restrictions, ongoing care needs, or recommendations for future treatment.

Include all elements: CC, HPI, exam findings, diagnostics, diagnosis, and plan of care.

3. Narrative Format

Present the medical information in a story-like, readable format, combining facts from multiple records.
Avoid simple lists; use complete sentences and transitions to show progression over time.

pages.title: 4. Notes for Accuracy and Consistency
pages.text:
Legal support help

4. Notes for Accuracy and Consistency

Include all key clinical elements (CC, HPI, exam findings, diagnostics, treatment, diagnosis, plan).
Be mindful of client preferences: some may prefer chronological DOS, others by provider.
Ensure consistency in terminology and accuracy in dates and treatment details.
Highlight any ongoing limitations or future care needs—important for damages or settlement purposes.

ALWAYS REMEMBER

The structure of the narrative may vary depending on the client’s template:
Some clients prefer each visit summarized by Date of Service (DOS).
Others prefer grouping summaries by provider.

pages.title: SOAP: Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan
pages.text:
Legal support help

The

S. - Subjective
O.- Objective
A. - Assessment
P. - Plan

is a standardized framework used in healthcare to document patient encounters in a clear, organized way. It ensures that clinical information is recorded logically and supports continuity of care, billing, and—crucially for legal work—causation and damages.

Process

In MedSum and Demand work, SOAP is essential because it:
Organizes raw medical records
Supports medical causation
Strengthens injury-to-treatment connections
Creates a defensible medical narrative

pages.title: S – Subjective (What the Patient Reports)
pages.text:
Legal support help

S – Subjective
(What the Patient Reports)

This section contains the patient’s personal complaints and history.
Includes:
Pain description (sharp, dull, radiating)
Pain level (e.g., 7/10)
Functional limitations (difficulty sitting, walking, sleeping)
Onset of symptoms
Mechanism of injury (MVA, slip and fall, assault, etc.)
Worsening or improvement over time

Legal Importance:
Establishes initial injury complaints
Shows consistency of symptoms
Helps prove the injury is not fabricated
Supports pain and suffering damages

Example:
“Patient reports constant low back pain rated 8/10, radiating to the right leg, beginning immediately after the motor vehicle accident.”

pages.title: O – Objective (What Can Be Verified)
pages.text:
Legal support help

O – Objective
(What Can Be Verified)

This section contains measurable and observable medical findings.
Includes:
Physical exam findings
MRI, X-ray, CT scan results
Range-of-motion tests
Swelling, bruising, muscle spasms
EMG/NCV studies
Vital signs related to injury

Legal Importance:
Provides hard proof of injury
Supports causation
Prevents the defense from arguing “subjective-only” pain
Strongly supports settlement value

Example:
“MRI of the lumbar spine revealed a 5mm disc herniation at L4-L5 with nerve root compression.”

pages.title: A – Assessment (Medical Diagnosis & Causation)
pages.text:
Legal support help

A – Assessment
(Medical Diagnosis & Causation)

The Assessment is the provider’s medical conclusion based on S + O.
Includes:
Medical diagnoses
Injury classification
Provider’s opinion on cause
Severity assessment
Correlation between accident and injury

Legal Importance:
This is where medical causation is established
Directly ties the incident to the injury
One of the most critical sections for demand letters


Example:
“The patient’s lumbar disc herniation is consistent with trauma from the reported motor vehicle collision.”

pages.title: P – Plan (Treatment & Future Care)
pages.text:
Legal support help

P – Plan
(Treatment & Future Care)

This section outlines what the provider will do next.
Includes:
Physical therapy
Chiropractic care
Pain management
Injections
Surgery recommendations
Medications
Follow-ups and referrals

Legal Importance:
Establishes economic damages
Supports future medical expenses
Justifies lien amounts
Increases demand value

Example:
“Recommend 12 weeks of physical therapy, lumbar epidural steroid injections, and orthopedic re-evaluation in 60 days.”

pages.title: Remember — 1. Use Past Tense and Active Voice
pages.text:
Legal support help

remember

1. Use Past Tense and Active Voice

Describe what the provider recommended, prescribed, or instructed the client to do, rather than using passive constructions.

Example:
Dr. Lee recommended physical therapy twice weekly for six weeks.
Physical therapy was recommended by Dr. Lee.

Example for follow-up:
Dr. Smith scheduled a follow-up visit in two weeks to reassess symptoms.
A follow-up visit was scheduled in two weeks.

pages.title: Remember — 2. Correct Use of Singular and Plural Nouns
pages.text:
Legal support help

remember

2. Correct Use of Singular and Plural Nouns

Verify that all nouns reflect proper singular or plural usage, particularly in formal names or possessives.

Example:
Mr. Jones’s MRI showed improvement. (singular possessive)
The therapists’ notes documented progress in range of motion.
(plural possessive)

pages.title: Remember — 3. Consistent Naming and Pronouns
pages.text:
Legal support help

remember

3. Consistent Naming and Pronouns

After introducing a person by their full name, refer to them consistently:
Clients: first name or Mr./Ms. last name.
Providers: Dr. last name, Nurse last name, PA last name.
Insured or other parties: same consistent reference throughout.
PRONOUNS should match the client’s gender and remain consistent.

Example:
✅ First reference: John Dela Cruz, reported lower back pain.
✅ Subsequent references: John reported mild discomfort during therapy.

ALWAYS REMEMBER

This depends on your client`s SOP of addressing the client in the summaries

pages.title: Remember — 4. Consistency Across the Document
pages.text:
Legal support help

remember

4. Consistency Across the Document

For each visit or treatment episode, include:
Maintain uniform formatting, tense, naming, and clinical terminology throughout the summary.
Avoid switching between first name, last name, or generic terms for the same person.
Ensure singular/plural nouns, dates, and pronouns are accurate throughout.

ALWAYS REMEMBER

This depends on your client`s SOP of addressing the client in the summaries

pages.title: Common Mistakes to Avoid — 1. Including Irrelevant Medical Details
pages.text:
Legal support help

Common Mistakes to Avoid

1. Including Irrelevant Medical Details

Problem: Adding unrelated medical history, unrelated diagnoses, or excessive detail can obscure the relevant facts.
Solution:
Focus on injuries and treatments directly related to the incident.
Summarize only other medical history if it affects diagnosis, treatment, or recovery.

Example:
The client has a history of seasonal allergies and mild eczema
unrelated to the accident.
The client had a pre-existing mild lumbar disc degeneration,
noted on prior imaging, which was aggravated by the accident.

pages.title: Common Mistakes to Avoid — 2. Using Overly Technical Jargon Without Explanation
pages.text:
Legal support help

Common Mistakes to Avoid

2. Using Overly Technical Jargon Without Explanation

Problem: Dense medical terminology can confuse non-medical readers like adjusters or attorneys.
Solution:
Use plain language where possible and briefly explain clinical terms.
Include the medical term followed by a short, clear description if needed.
Example:
MRI revealed an L4-L5 herniated nucleus pulposus.
MRI revealed a herniated disc at L4-L5, which is a bulging of the disc
between the fourth and fifth lumbar vertebrae.

pages.title: Common Mistakes to Avoid — 3. Omitting Dates, Providers, or Critical Events
pages.text:
Legal support help

Common Mistakes to Avoid

3. Omitting Dates, Providers, or Critical Events

Problem: Missing key dates, provider names, or significant events can make the summary incomplete and reduce credibility.
Solution:
Always include:
Date of service (DOS) and Provider name and title
Critical events such as surgeries, ER visits, diagnostic results, or therapy.
Example:
Client underwent surgery and therapy afterward.
On March 15, 2025, Dr. Emily Lee performed a lumbar discectomy.
Post-surgery, the client attended 12 PT sessions with PT John
Ramirez.

pages.title: Common Mistakes to Avoid — 4. Mixing Pre-Existing and Incident-Related Injuries
pages.text:
Legal support help

Common Mistakes to Avoid

4. Mixing Pre-Existing Conditions with Incident-Related Injuries

Problem: Blurring the line between prior conditions and new injuries can weaken the claim or confuse readers.
Solution:
Clearly distinguish between pre-existing conditions and incident-related injuries.
Highlight aggravation caused by the incident when applicable.
Example:
Client had chronic back pain and lower back pain after the accident.
Client had mild pre-existing lumbar disc degeneration, which was
exacerbated by the accident, resulting in acute lower back
pain and radiculopathy.
